title: Rice for a Hangover: Does It Help? Congee, Curd Rice, and More
excerpt: Is rice good for a hangover? Why bland rice settles a queasy stomach, why congee and curd rice work so well, white vs brown rice, and what rice can't fix.
metaDescription: Is rice good for a hangover? Why plain rice settles a queasy stomach, how congee and curd rice help, white vs brown rice, and what rice can't fix.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** rice is a good hangover food, but it isn't a cure. Plain white rice is bland, low in fat and fiber, and easy to digest, so it tends to sit well on a stomach that alcohol has irritated. It gives you a quick, gentle source of carbohydrate when your blood sugar may be running low, and cooked rice carries a fair amount of water with it. Served as a soupy rice porridge (congee) or mixed with yogurt (curd rice), it also adds fluid, salt, and in the yogurt version some protein. What rice can't do is clear alcohol from your body faster, undo the inflammation and poor sleep behind a hangover, or stop a headache by itself. It's a smart, easy meal that helps you feel more like yourself, not a remedy.

**The quick version of what to do:** if your stomach is unsettled, start with a small bowl of plain white rice or a thin rice porridge with a pinch of salt. Sip water or an electrolyte drink alongside it. Once that stays down, add something with protein, like an egg, some chicken, tofu, or a spoonful of plain yogurt. Skip the heavy fried rice and extra-spicy toppings until your stomach has settled. If you're doing fine on food but still feel rough, the things that actually move the needle are fluids, rest, and time.

> **When to see a doctor.** Most hangovers fade within a day with food, fluids, and rest. Get medical help right away if you or someone you're with can't keep any liquids down for several hours, is vomiting repeatedly or vomiting blood, has severe stomach pain, is confused or hard to wake, has slow or irregular breathing, has a seizure, or has bluish or very pale skin. Those can be signs of alcohol poisoning, severe dehydration, or another serious problem, and you should call 911 (or your local emergency number). If you drink most days and feel shaky, sweaty, anxious, or sick when you stop, that's not an ordinary hangover. It can be a sign of alcohol withdrawal, which can become dangerous, so talk to a doctor rather than waiting it out. This article is general information, not medical advice.

## Is Rice Good for a Hangover?

For most people, yes. Rice isn't special in a magical sense. It's useful because of what it is and what it isn't.

**What rice is:** a starchy, simple, mild food. A cup of cooked white rice is mostly carbohydrate with a small amount of protein and almost no fat. It's one of the most widely eaten foods in the world, and in many countries it's the default thing people eat when they feel unwell.

**What rice isn't:** greasy, acidic, spicy, high in fiber, or strongly flavored. Those are exactly the qualities that tend to bother a stomach that's still irritated from a night of drinking.

That combination is why rice shows up on so many "gentle food" lists. It gives your body fuel without asking your stomach to do much work. If you've ever had a bowl of plain rice when you were sick and thought "that's the first thing I've been able to eat all day," you already know the appeal.

The catch is that a hangover isn't one problem. It's a mix of dehydration, low blood sugar for some people, an irritated gut, poor sleep, inflammation, and the after-effects of alcohol's breakdown products. Rice helps with a couple of those pieces. It doesn't touch the others.

## Why Rice Helps: What's Happening in Your Body

### 1. It's easy on an irritated stomach

Alcohol irritates the lining of the stomach and can increase acid production. That's a big part of why the morning after can bring nausea, a sour or burning stomach, or a lack of appetite. Our guide on [stomach pain after drinking](/never-hungover/stomach-pain-after-drinking) explains this in more detail.

When your stomach is in that state, the foods that tend to go down best are bland, low in fat, and low in fiber. Fat slows down how fast your stomach empties, which can make nausea linger. Lots of fiber is harder to digest quickly. Strong spices and acidic foods can add to the burning feeling. White rice avoids all of these. It's about as neutral as food gets.

### 2. It gives you carbohydrate when blood sugar may be low

Your liver normally keeps your blood sugar steady by releasing stored sugar and by making new glucose between meals. Processing alcohol gets in the way of that second job. After a night of drinking, especially if you didn't eat much, some people end up with lower blood sugar than usual. That can add to the tired, weak, shaky, foggy feeling of a hangover.

Rice is mostly starch, and white rice in particular breaks down into glucose fairly quickly. That's usually a drawback in everyday eating, because it can cause a quick rise in blood sugar. On a hangover morning, a quick, easy source of carbohydrate can actually be useful. It's one reason toast, crackers, and rice all show up in hangover advice. If you want to read more about the sugar side of this, see our guide to [sugar for a hangover](/never-hungover/sugar-for-hangover).

The research on low blood sugar and hangovers is mixed. Studies haven't found that blood sugar levels neatly predict how bad a hangover feels. But eating some carbohydrate is a reasonable, low-risk step, and it beats skipping breakfast.

### 3. Cooked rice carries water

Rice soaks up a lot of water as it cooks. Cooked white rice is roughly two-thirds water by weight. That won't rehydrate you on its own, and you still need to drink, but a bowl of rice is a more hydrating meal than dry toast or crackers. A thin rice porridge like congee goes further, because it's mostly liquid.

Alcohol makes you lose more fluid than usual, mainly by suppressing a hormone (vasopressin, also called antidiuretic hormone) that normally tells your kidneys to hold onto water. If you're also sweating or vomiting, you lose more. Food that carries water and salt, like a salted rice porridge, helps a little alongside your drinks. For the full picture, see [how to rehydrate after drinking](/never-hungover/how-to-rehydrate-after-drinking).

### 4. It's a good base for the things that help more

Plain rice is low in protein, vitamins, and minerals compared with many other foods. Its real strength is as a base. Add an egg, some broth, a little chicken or fish, yogurt, or cooked vegetables, and you get a balanced meal that's still gentle. Protein and a bit of fat help keep your blood sugar steadier over the next few hours, so you don't crash again by early afternoon.

## Congee: The Classic Hangover Rice Dish

Congee is rice cooked in a lot of water or broth until the grains break down into a soft, soupy porridge. It goes by many names. It's called jook in Cantonese and Korean, zhou or xifan in Mandarin, okayu in Japanese, cháo in Vietnamese, lugaw in the Philippines, and kanji in parts of India. Across much of Asia it's the food people reach for when they're sick, recovering, or simply need something gentle, and many people eat it the morning after drinking for the same reasons.

Congee may be the best form of rice for a hangover, for a few reasons:

- **It's mostly liquid.** A bowl of congee is as much a drink as a meal, so it helps with fluids while you eat.
- **It's very easy to digest.** The long cooking breaks the rice down so thoroughly that there's very little left for your stomach to work on.
- **It takes salt well.** Congee is usually seasoned, often cooked in broth. That salt replaces some of what you lose through extra urination and sweating, and it helps your body hold onto the fluid you drink.
- **It's easy to build up.** Start plain. Add toppings as your appetite returns.

### Good congee toppings for a hangover

- A soft-boiled or poached egg, or a salted or century egg if you like them
- Shredded chicken or a little flaked fish
- A splash of soy sauce and a few drops of sesame oil
- Sliced green onion and fresh ginger (ginger has some evidence for easing nausea)
- Cooked greens or mushrooms
- A pickled plum (umeboshi), which is a traditional okayu topping in Japan

Go easy on deep-fried toppings like fried dough sticks if your stomach is touchy. They're traditional and delicious, but the fat can make nausea worse.

### A quick congee method

You don't need a special recipe. Use about one part rice to eight to ten parts water or broth. Bring it to a boil, turn it down to a low simmer, and stir now and then for 45 minutes to an hour and a half until it's thick and creamy. A rice cooker with a porridge setting or a slow cooker works too. If you already have leftover cooked rice, you can make a fast version by simmering it in broth for 15 to 20 minutes and mashing it a bit as it cooks. If you plan ahead, a pot made the night before is easy to reheat in the morning.

## Curd Rice: South India's Cooling Comfort Food

Curd rice is a South Indian dish of cooked rice mixed with plain yogurt (called "curd" in India), usually salted and often finished with a quick tempering of mustard seeds, curry leaves, ginger, and sometimes green chili, fried briefly in a little oil. It's called thayir sadam in Tamil and daddojanam in Telugu. It's often eaten at the end of a meal or on hot days because it feels cooling and soothing, and it's a common choice when someone's stomach is upset.

As a hangover food, curd rice has a lot going for it:

- **It's gentle.** Soft rice and yogurt are both mild and easy to eat when you don't have much appetite.
- **It adds protein.** Yogurt brings protein that plain rice lacks, which helps keep you full and your energy steadier.
- **It brings fluid and salt.** The yogurt and salt add both. Many people also thin it with a little milk or water.
- **It contains live cultures, if the yogurt does.** Yogurt with live and active cultures adds probiotic bacteria. There's no good evidence that probiotics treat a hangover, but some people find yogurt soothing on an upset stomach. Our post on [yogurt for a hangover](/never-hungover/yogurt-for-hangover) covers what the research does and doesn't show.

If your stomach is very sensitive, leave out the green chili and keep the tempering light. Plain rice, plain yogurt, and a pinch of salt is a perfectly good version on a rough morning.

## White Rice vs Brown Rice for a Hangover

On a normal day, brown rice is the more nutritious choice. It keeps the bran and germ, so it has more fiber, more magnesium, and more B vitamins than white rice. Alcohol can increase how much of some of these nutrients you lose, so that's a point in brown rice's favor.

On a hangover morning, though, white rice is often the better choice, at least at first:

| | White rice | Brown rice |
|---|---|---|
| How easy to digest | Very easy | Harder, because of the extra fiber |
| Speed of energy | Faster | Slower and steadier |
| Fiber | Low | Higher |
| Magnesium and B vitamins | Lower (unless enriched) | Higher |
| Best for | A queasy, sensitive stomach | A settled stomach and a later meal |

A simple rule: if you feel sick to your stomach, start with white rice or congee. If your stomach feels fine and you're just tired and run down, brown rice with some protein is a good choice for a steadier meal. Many white rice products sold in the US are enriched with some B vitamins, which narrows the gap a little.

## Rice and the BRAT Diet

Rice is the "R" in the BRAT diet: bananas, rice, applesauce, and toast. For years, BRAT was standard advice for people recovering from stomach bugs and diarrhea, because all four foods are bland and easy to digest.

Doctors have moved away from strict BRAT diets, mainly because those four foods on their own are low in protein, fat, and many nutrients. Current advice for children with stomach illness, for example, is generally to return to a normal, age-appropriate diet once they can eat, rather than restricting them to BRAT foods. The underlying idea still holds for adults with a short-term upset stomach, though: bland, starchy foods are a sensible first step, and then you add other foods as you feel better.

For a hangover, that translates to: rice, bananas, or toast are fine to start, but don't stay on bland starch all day. Add protein and fluids early. If you want ideas for the other BRAT foods, see our guides to [bananas for a hangover](/never-hungover/bananas-for-hangover) and [toast and crackers for a hangover](/never-hungover/toast-and-crackers-for-hangover).

## Is Rice Good for Diarrhea After Drinking?

Loose stools are a common, unpleasant part of the morning after. Alcohol speeds up how fast things move through your gut and reduces how well your intestines absorb water, so more water stays in your stool. Our guide to [diarrhea after drinking](/never-hungover/diarrhea-after-drinking) explains the causes.

Plain white rice is a reasonable food to eat when you have diarrhea. It's low in fiber and fat, it doesn't irritate the gut, and many people find it helps them feel more settled. It won't stop diarrhea on its own, but it's unlikely to make it worse.

The more important thing is fluid. Diarrhea pulls water and electrolytes (salts like sodium and potassium) out of your body. Drink water steadily, and consider an oral rehydration solution or an electrolyte drink if you've had several loose stools.

You may have heard of rice water, the starchy water left after boiling rice, as a home remedy for diarrhea. Rice-based oral rehydration solutions have been studied in children and adults with severe diarrheal illness, and they've been used in some medical settings. Those are carefully made solutions with the right amounts of salt and starch, though, not the leftover water from a pot of rice. A bowl of salted congee gets you much of the same practical benefit (starch, fluid, and salt) in a form that's easy to make at home.

**See a doctor if** diarrhea lasts more than two days, you see blood or black, tarry stool, you have a high fever, you have severe belly pain, or you show signs of dehydration such as very little urine, dizziness when you stand, or a racing heart.

## Fried Rice, Rice Bowls, and Other Ways to Eat It

Not every rice dish is equally gentle. Here's a quick guide to common options:

- **Plain steamed rice with a pinch of salt:** the gentlest option. Good when you can barely face food.
- **Congee or rice porridge:** the best all-round choice. Gentle, hydrating, and easy to add protein to.
- **Curd rice:** gentle, adds protein, cooling. A great choice if you like yogurt.
- **Rice with an egg, or "rice and eggs":** a simple, balanced breakfast. Eggs add protein and some nutrients. See our post on [eggs for a hangover](/never-hungover/eggs-for-hangover).
- **Rice in soup:** a bowl of broth-based soup with rice, such as chicken and rice soup, adds fluid and salt. Korea's hangover soups (haejang-guk) are traditionally served with a bowl of rice. Our guide to the [Korean hangover soup](/never-hungover/korean-hangover-soup) and roundup of the [best soups for a hangover](/never-hungover/best-soups-for-hangover) have more ideas.
- **Japanese ochazuke:** rice with hot green tea or dashi broth poured over it, often topped with pickled plum, salmon, or seaweed. It's light, salty, and soupy, and it's often described as a good meal after a night out.
- **Fried rice:** fine if your stomach is already settled and you're hungry. It's cooked in oil, often with soy sauce, eggs, and vegetables, so it's more filling. But the extra fat can be a problem if you're still nauseous. Our guide to [greasy food for a hangover](/never-hungover/greasy-food-hangover) explains why a big greasy meal often helps less than people expect.
- **Burritos and rice bowls with heavy toppings:** satisfying, but cheese, sour cream, fried meat, and hot sauce can be hard on an irritated stomach. Save them for when you feel better.

## Should You Eat Rice Before Drinking?

Eating before you drink matters more than anything you eat the morning after. Food in your stomach slows how fast alcohol passes into your small intestine, where most of it is absorbed. That gives you a slower, lower peak in blood alcohol than drinking on an empty stomach. Our guide on [drinking on an empty stomach](/never-hungover/drinking-on-an-empty-stomach) goes into the details.

A rice-based meal is a good choice before a night out, but rice alone isn't ideal. Plain starch leaves your stomach relatively quickly. A meal that combines carbohydrate with protein, some fat, and fiber slows things down more and keeps you full longer. Think rice with chicken or fish and vegetables, a burrito bowl, a curry with rice, or sushi with some protein-rich pieces. For more ideas, see [what to eat before drinking alcohol](/never-hungover/what-to-eat-before-drinking-alcohol-evidence-based-guide).

Eating doesn't make you immune to the effects of alcohol. It slows absorption, it doesn't cancel it out. Pacing and the total amount you drink still matter most.

## What Rice Can't Fix

Rice is a helpful food, but it's worth being clear about its limits so you don't expect too much from it:

- **It doesn't clear alcohol faster.** Your liver breaks down alcohol at a fairly fixed rate. Food eaten the next morning doesn't speed that up.
- **It doesn't address inflammation.** Research suggests that part of what makes a hangover feel so bad is the body's inflammatory response to alcohol. Rice has no meaningful effect on that.
- **It doesn't fix poor sleep.** Alcohol disrupts sleep, especially in the second half of the night. That's a big reason you feel wrecked the next day, and no breakfast fixes it.
- **It won't rehydrate you by itself.** Even congee is only part of the solution. You still need to drink fluids.
- **It doesn't treat a headache.** Food can help if low blood sugar or hunger is adding to the headache, but it isn't a pain reliever. For more on headaches specifically, see our guide on [hangover headache relief](/never-hungover/hangover-headache-fast-relief-methods-2025).

There's also no evidence that rice works better than other bland, starchy foods. Toast, crackers, oatmeal, bananas, and potatoes do similar jobs. Rice is a good option, especially if you already like it and have it in the house. It isn't uniquely good.

## A Simple Rice-Based Hangover Morning

Here's a practical plan for the morning after, built around rice:

1. **Start with fluids.** Drink a glass of water or an electrolyte drink as soon as you're up. Keep sipping through the morning rather than gulping a lot at once, which can upset a queasy stomach.
2. **Eat something small and bland.** A small bowl of plain rice or thin congee with a little salt. Eat slowly.
3. **Add protein once it stays down.** An egg, some chicken, tofu, fish, or a scoop of plain yogurt.
4. **Add flavor and vegetables later.** Ginger, green onion, a splash of soy sauce, cooked greens.
5. **Rest.** Sleep or take it easy if you can. Time is the main thing that ends a hangover.
6. **Have a proper meal later in the day.** Once your appetite is back, a balanced meal helps you recover fully.

If you've got leftover rice in the fridge, reheat it until it's steaming hot all the way through. Cooked rice can carry bacteria (notably *Bacillus cereus*) whose spores survive cooking. If cooked rice sits at room temperature for hours, those bacteria can grow and make toxins that cause vomiting and diarrhea, and reheating doesn't destroy those toxins. Cool leftover rice quickly, keep it in the fridge, and eat it within a day or so. Food poisoning on top of a hangover is a miserable combination.

## Where Supplements Fit In

Food helps you recover once a hangover has arrived. Some people also look at supplements to support their body around drinking. The most commonly discussed is **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been used in traditional Chinese medicine for a long time.

Here's an honest summary of the evidence. Most of the research on DHM comes from lab and animal studies, which suggest it may support the way the body processes alcohol and may help protect liver cells. Human research is limited. There's a small amount of clinical data, including a 2015 randomized trial in people with fatty liver disease that found improvements in some liver markers, but there is no good evidence from large human trials that DHM prevents hangovers. If you want to try it, the usual approach is to take it with water around the time you drink, and to treat it as one small piece of a plan that still includes food, water, pacing, and sleep. It doesn't make heavy drinking safe.

Popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20), which combines DHM with other ingredients, and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how much people typically take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. If you take prescription medication, check with a doctor or pharmacist before adding any supplement.

For a broader look at foods that help, see our guide to the [best foods for a hangover](/never-hungover/best-foods-for-hangover), and for habits that reduce how bad the next morning is, see [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

## The Bottom Line

- Rice is a good hangover food because it's bland, low in fat and fiber, easy to digest, and gives you quick carbohydrate.
- **Congee** (rice porridge) is probably the best form, since it adds fluid and salt along with gentle food.
- **Curd rice** (rice with yogurt) is another great choice that adds protein and feels cooling.
- **White rice** is easier on an upset stomach. **Brown rice** is more nutritious once your stomach is settled.
- Rice is fine for diarrhea after drinking, but fluids and electrolytes matter more.
- Add protein once your stomach can handle it, and keep drinking water.
- Rice doesn't clear alcohol, fix poor sleep, or stop inflammation. Food, fluids, rest, and time do the heavy lifting.
- Get medical help for repeated vomiting, inability to keep liquids down, confusion, trouble breathing, or seizures.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is rice good for a hangover?**

Yes, for most people. Plain white rice is bland, low in fat and fiber, and easy to digest, so it tends to sit well on a stomach that's irritated from drinking. It provides quick carbohydrate if your blood sugar is low, and cooked rice contains a lot of water. It isn't a cure, though. It won't clear alcohol faster or fix poor sleep, so pair it with fluids, protein, and rest.

**Is congee good for a hangover?**

Congee, or rice porridge, is one of the best forms of rice for a hangover. It's very easy to digest, it's mostly liquid so it helps with fluids, and it's usually seasoned with salt or cooked in broth, which helps replace some of what you lose. Start with a plain bowl and add an egg, chicken, ginger, or green onion once your stomach settles.

**Is curd rice good for a hangover?**

Curd rice, cooked rice mixed with plain yogurt and salt, is a gentle, cooling dish that many people find soothing on an upset stomach. The yogurt adds protein and fluid, and yogurt with live cultures adds probiotic bacteria, though there's no good evidence that probiotics treat a hangover. Keep the spices mild if your stomach is sensitive.

**Is white rice or brown rice better for a hangover?**

White rice is usually better first thing if your stomach is queasy, because it's lower in fiber and easier to digest. Brown rice has more fiber, magnesium, and B vitamins, so it's a good choice for a later meal once your stomach has settled and you want steadier energy.

**Does rice help with diarrhea after drinking?**

Plain white rice is a sensible food to eat when you have diarrhea, because it's low in fiber and fat and doesn't irritate the gut. It won't stop diarrhea on its own. Replacing fluids and electrolytes matters more, so drink water steadily and consider an electrolyte drink. See a doctor if diarrhea lasts more than two days, you see blood, or you have signs of dehydration.

**Is fried rice good for a hangover?**

Fried rice is fine if your stomach is already settled and you're hungry, since it combines carbohydrate with egg and vegetables. But it's cooked in oil, and fatty food can make nausea worse and slow down how fast your stomach empties. If you still feel queasy, plain rice or congee is a better first choice.

**Should I eat rice before drinking?**

Eating before you drink helps slow how fast alcohol is absorbed. A rice-based meal is a good choice, but rice on its own is less effective than a meal that also includes protein, fat, and fiber, such as rice with chicken or fish and vegetables. Food slows absorption but doesn't cancel the effects of alcohol, so pacing still matters most.

**Is it safe to eat leftover rice when hungover?**

Yes, as long as it was stored properly. Cooked rice can carry bacteria whose spores survive cooking and can grow if the rice is left at room temperature for hours, causing vomiting and diarrhea. Cool leftover rice quickly, keep it in the fridge, eat it within about a day, and reheat it until it's steaming hot all the way through.
